tools.name: mcp__t3-code__schedule_task
tools.description: Create persistent work in the app scheduler that runs even when no turn is active. Pass schedule as a STRUCTURED OBJECT, never JSON text. Timers: {type:'interval', everyMs:3600000} is hourly; {type:'fixed_time', timeOfDay:'09:00', weekdays:[1,2,3,4,5]} is weekday mornings; report the returned nextRunAt. Webhooks: {type:'webhook'} runs once per request to a generated URL. The run sees the request ONLY through prompt placeholders: {{body.path}} (e.g. {{body.action}}, {{body.release.tag_name}}), {{headers.name}}, {{query.name}}, {{body}}, or {{request}} (method, headers with credentials redacted, and body). For a sender that signs requests, first call request_secret so the user enters the secret privately (never ask for it in chat or invent one), then set signature with the returned secretRef, e.g. GitHub: {type:'webhook', signature:{header:'x-hub-signature-256', encoding:'hex', prefix:'sha256=', secretRef}}. The result's webhookUrl is the public URL to give the user; if it is absent, this environment has no T3 Connect managed tunnel, so tell the user to enable T3 Connect remote access rather than sharing a path. Omit projectId for this thread's project. In this thread's project, runs post into THIS thread by default (bindToCurrentThread=true), which suits an orchestrator that sees every trigger, delegates work, and can dedupe against what is in flight; use false only when the user wants a fresh top-level thread per run. Elsewhere each run launches a fresh thread. Provider, model, and runtime settings inherit from this thread, or from the project default when there is no calling thread.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_thread_launch
tools.description: Create an ordinary TOP-LEVEL thread with an explicit workspace binding before its agent starts. Use this when the user requests independent work, a new thread, or a PR stack in its own worktree; use delegate_task for child subagents. Set workspaceStrategy to {type:"worktree",baseRef:"parent-branch",branch:"new-branch",startFromOrigin:false} for a new worktree based on local commits, or {type:"existing_worktree",worktreePath:"/absolute/path",branch:"existing-branch"} to use an existing checkout. For upstream commits, set startFromOrigin:true. Omitted workspaceStrategy means the project root, NOT the caller's worktree. Omit projectId/modelSelection/modes to inherit those settings from the calling thread; a caller outside a T3 thread must pass projectId and gets the project's default model. Set scratch:true instead of projectId for a thread without a project: it runs in a fresh folder of its own, outside any repository. Put the task in message. Do not ask the agent to create its own worktree via shell: that does not update the thread binding. Each call creates a new launch with no retry key; retain threadId and use t3_thread_read/t3_thread_wait to follow preparation. To link a thread for the user, write `[title](t3-thread://v1/<threadId>)` with the threadId exactly as returned, not URL-encoded; T3 Code shows the thread's current title. After errors or lost responses, inspect t3_thread_list before retrying. Attachments must be pending uploads. The new thread may not run with broader runtime or interaction modes than the caller: the calling T3 thread's own modes, or the permission mode an outside agent was approved with.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__t3_worktree_handoff
tools.description: Needs an agent running inside a T3 thread. Move this agent thread into a new git worktree. To launch a separate agent already bound to a new or existing worktree, use t3_thread_launch with workspaceStrategy instead. Creates the worktree branch (optionally from origin), re-points the thread at the worktree, and by default runs the project's setup script there. Changing the workspace detaches the live provider session, so the current turn ends shortly after the handoff is recorded; call this as the last action of the turn. To keep working after the handoff, pass continuationPrompt with the remaining work: it is queued as the thread's next message and starts a new turn inside the worktree with the conversation preserved. Without it the thread stays idle until the next message. The worktree is not removed automatically when the thread is deleted. Fails if the thread is already attached to a worktree.

I can't reproduce the changelog verbatim because of the quoting limits, but here is a close summary with short exact quotes.

## v0.7.0 (2026-10-14)

**Breaking changes**
- The minimum runtime is now Node.js 22 ("require Node.js 22 or newer").
- Request payload types are no longer exported.

**Features (image/multimodal/asset)**
- **Images (experimental):** These are enabled via the `TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true` header. You create them with `image()` or `Image.fromBase64()`. They can go in `state`, question instructions, or criteria. You can embed them in text using `withAssets` / `withAssets.join`, or refer to them by custom names in `assets`.
- **`box` questions:** These "locate what their instructions describe in an image" and are used with the `jev-preview` model.
- **Compression:** Request bodies of 1 KiB or larger are zstd-compressed on Node.js 22.15+. You can opt out with `compression: false`.

**Bug fixes**
- Null token counts in usage are now permitted.
- Additional request validation checks were added.
- Invalid requests now reject the returned promise rather than throwing.
- Score criteria lists constructed at runtime are accepted.
- An unhandled rejection on Node.js 22 was fixed. It happened when a request timed out or was aborted mid-body.

## v0.6.0 (2026-09-15)

**Breaking change**
- `Score.criteria` is now an ordered sequence, not a dictionary keyed by integers.

## v0.5.7 (2026-09-11)

- This was the first public release of the TypeSafe JavaScript/TypeScript SDK. Docs: https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/js-sdk

I can't reproduce the whole page verbatim because quotes are limited to 125 characters. Here is a summary of every topic, with short excerpts.

## Installation & env vars
- Requires Node.js 22+. Install with `npm install @typesafe-ai/sdk`.
- Set the `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` environment variable, then create the client with `new TypeSafeClient()`.
- The package ships ESM, CommonJS and TypeScript declarations. Answer types are inferred from your questions.

## Making requests
Call `client.systemOne({ state, questions })`. The quickstart classifies a support ticket:
```ts
category: choice("What is this ticket about?", { billing: null, technical: null, other: null })
```

# TypeSafe System One: Images

I can't reproduce the code samples verbatim because quotes must stay under 125 characters. Below I describe them closely and include short excerpts.

## Status and enabling
- Images and Box questions are a **"Dreamer-ready"** feature. They are meant for prototypes, not production. The request format, answers, limits and accuracy may change between releases. Feedback goes to Discord.
- The feature is off by default. Every request that contains an image or a Box question must include the header `TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true`. Without it, the request returns `400`.
- Jev 1.13 and 1.14 accept images. Box questions require Jev 1.14.

## How references work
- Each image is listed once in a top-level `assets` map. The map key is a reference string.
- You put that string wherever the image belongs: as a whole string value or inside a longer string. The model "receives the image in its place."
- **Asset fields:**
  - `type`: optional, but must be `"image"` if present.
  - `part`: the name of the multipart file part.
  - `data_base64`: required unless `part` is set. Use the standard alphabet with `=` padding, no whitespace, and no `data:` prefix.
  - `format`: `png`, `jpg` or `jpeg`, lowercase. Required with base64, optional with `part`.
  - If an asset has both `part` and `data_base64`, `part` wins.
- **Reference rules:**
  - References match as plain text anywhere in the request's strings. A short key like `cat` could also hit `category`, so a fresh UUID per image per request is safest.
  - Every asset must be referenced somewhere, or the request returns `400`.
  - Whole-value matches are applied first. In longer strings, replacement runs left to right with no overlapping matches.
  - Each use of a reference adds another copy of the image to what the model reads, and every copy counts toward the expanded-request limit.
  - Object keys are never replaced. Choice option names and question IDs stay as text, so put the reference in the option's description instead.
  - Answers show the reference, not the image (for example, in a Score `legend`).
  - Each reference can be at most 1,024 UTF-8 bytes, and all references together at most 65,536 bytes. A reference can't be empty or whitespace-only.

**Example request (lost dog):**
- `state.photo` holds a found-dog reference.
- A `same_dog` Noul question embeds the poster's reference in its instructions: "Is the dog in \`photo\` the same dog as in this picture: 77b0d4a1-poster?"
- There is also a `has_collar` Noul and a `coat` Choice with options short, long and curly.
- Questions refer to state images by name or path in backticks.

## SDK usage
**Python:**
- Import `Choice, Image, Noul, TypeSafeClient` from `typesafe_sdk`.
- Inside `with TypeSafeClient() as client:`, call `client.system_one(...)` with:
  - `state={"door": Image(Path("door-camera.jpg"))}`
  - Noul `person_present` and Choice `carrying` (package, bag, nothing)
  - `extra_headers={"TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images": "true"}`
- Print `result.answers`.

**JavaScript:**
- Import `openAsBlob` from `node:fs`, and `choice, image, noul, TypeSafeClient` from `@typesafe-ai/sdk`.
- Build the image with `image(await openAsBlob("door-camera.jpg"))`.
- Call `client.systemOne({state:{door}, questions:{...}}, { headers: { "TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images": "true" } })`.

The SDK generates references and uploads the files for you. The SDK guides cover inline images and custom references.

## Raw HTTP
Multipart is recommended because base64 inflates each image by about a third, and that counts toward the 32 MiB body limit.

**Multipart (curl):**
- POST to `https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` with the Bearer auth header and the images header.
- `-F 'request={...};type=application/json'`, where `assets` maps `"a3f1c2e8-door"` to `{"type":"image","part":"door-photo"}`.
- `-F 'door-photo=@door-camera.jpg;type=image/jpeg'`.

**Multipart rules:**
- The first part must be named `request` and hold the JSON. The name `request` is reserved.
- Part names must be unique and non-empty.
- Image part content types: `image/png`, `image/jpeg`, `image/jpg`, `application/octet-stream`, or none. Anything else returns `400`.
- Each file part belongs to exactly one asset. An unused part, a part shared by two assets, or a missing part all return `400`.
- To reuse an image, repeat its reference rather than uploading it again.

**Base64 (Python `requests`):**
- An `image_asset(path)` helper picks png or jpg from the file extension and base64-encodes the file.
- It returns `str(uuid.uuid4())` plus the asset dict.
- The script posts JSON containing state, assets and the same two questions, then prints `response.json()["answers"]`.

## Where images can go
- **State:**
  - Images become part of the state, so every question is evaluated against them.
  - Images can be mixed with text, nested, or labeled.
  - Example: a `frames` array with `seconds_ago` and `frame` fields, oldest first. A question can address one frame as `` `frames[2].frame` ``.
- **Instructions:**
  - The image is sent only with that question, and is resent for each question that includes it.
  - If several questions need the same image, put it in the state once to save tokens and stay under the limits.
- **Criteria:**
  - Choice options, Score levels, and Noul `true`/`false` definitions can all include images.
  - A gesture Choice example uses:
    - `thumbs_up` as a bare reference
    - `open_palm` as a description plus an `examples` array
    - `fist` as a reference
    - `none` as text only
  - `description` and `examples` are just illustrative key names; any structure is accepted.
  - Score levels can each have an example picture.
  - Noul criteria can define true/false with pictures.
- **Structured data:** references work at any nesting level, for example `` `lineup[2]` `` or `` `faces.happy` ``.

## Patterns
| Pattern | Image placement |
|---|---|
| Compare a photo to a known picture | Known picture in instructions, photo in state |
| Define Choice options by example pictures | Criteria |
| Detect what changed using previous frames | State |
| Look closer: ask about a small copy first, then a larger copy or full-resolution crop only if needed | State |
| Search a large image: tile it, offer the tiles as Choice options, recurse on the chosen tile | Criteria |
| Find where something is with a Box question | State, optionally a target picture in instructions |

## Limits
All ranges are inclusive. Images outside them are rejected, never resized.

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Format | PNG or JPEG stills only; animated PNG is rejected |
| File size | 16 MiB per file (decoded size for base64) |
| Width and height | 280–1568 px each |
| Total pixels | 78,400–2,458,624 |
| Request body | 32 MiB, including JSON, base64 and multipart framing; headers excluded; compression doesn't help |
| All distinct processed images | 32 MiB combined. Re-encoding can make an image larger than the upload |
| Expanded request | 32 MiB after all references are substituted. One 10 MiB image used four times exceeds it |

- If any image is rejected, the whole request fails, with no partial answers.
- The number of images per request is bounded by these limits and the model's context length.
- Images have no separate rate limits.

## Preparing images
- Downscale so the longest side is at most 1568 px; a 12 MP phone photo becomes 1568×1176. Upscale or pad images that are too small.
- Rotate the pixels upright yourself. The API strips all metadata (EXIF, color profiles, comments) and ignores EXIF orientation.
- Convert GIF, WebP, HEIC, animations and video to a still PNG or JPEG.
- Prefer 8-bit baseline JPEG; re-save progressive JPEGs as baseline.
- If the API rejects a file that opens fine locally, re-export it.

**Pillow example:**
- `ImageOps.exif_transpose` to rotate the pixels upright.
- `thumbnail((1568, 1568))`, which only shrinks.
- `convert("RGB").save(..., "JPEG", quality=90)`.

## Tokens and pricing
- Images count as input tokens at the normal input price, with no separate image fee.
- They are included in `usage.input_tokens` and count toward the context length.
- Guidance on estimating image tokens is "coming soon."

## Errors
| Status | Cause |
|---|---|
| `400` | Images header missing |
| `400` | Bad file: wrong format, damaged or animated, too small, unreferenced asset, bad base64 or format, empty reference, or a multipart rule violation |
| `400 max_tokens_exceeded` | Images plus text exceed the context length |
| `413` | A size limit is exceeded: file, dimensions, total pixels, body, combined images, expanded request, or reference lengths |

If a request has several problems, only one is reported.

# TypeSafe Jev Models: Summary

**Endpoint:** All models are served through `POST /v1/systemone`. The `model` field in the request chooses which one runs.

## Current models

| | Jev 1.14 | Jev 1.13 |
|---|---|---|
| Model ID | `jev-1.14.0` | `jev-1.13.0` |
| Price | $42 per billion tokens ($0.042 per million) | Same |
| Context | 64k per request / 32k per question | Same |
| Input | Text only | Text only |

- Jev 1.14 is the newest release, available starting October 14, 2026.
- **Pricing:** You pay only for input tokens. "Output tokens are free."

## Images and Box
- **Images:** The page does not mention image support. It lists text as the only input. Audio and video are explicitly unsupported and must be converted to text or structured fields first.
- **Box:** The page does not mention Box at all.

## Context length
- **Per-request limit:** the `state` plus all questions combined.
- **Per-question limit:** the `state` plus any single question.
- There is no cap on the number of questions, as long as the request fits both limits.
- **Long context:** This is off by default and works on both versions. To enable it, add the header `TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: true` to each request. Both limits then rise to 262k tokens.
  - The per-token price stays the same.
  - The docs warn it is "slower and less accurate than staying within the default limits."

## Aliases and how they resolve

| Alias | Resolves to | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `jev-latest` | `jev-1.13.0` | The newest stable, official release. It is the SDK default and is used in the doc examples. |
| `jev-preview` | `jev-1.14.0` | The newest release of any kind, including preview builds. |

- Aliases move when new versions ship, so results can change without any code changes on your side.
- Each response's `model` field reports the exact versioned ID that answered.
- If you have tuned confidence thresholds, pin a versioned ID instead of an alias.

## Deprecation
The page gives no deprecation details or timelines.

## Other notes
- **Listing models:** `GET /v1/models` currently returns only the aliases. Versioned IDs are still accepted in requests even though they are not listed.
- **Rate limits:** Limits are set per organization, in tokens per second and requests per second. Exceeding them returns a 429 error, and the SDKs retry automatically with backoff.
- **Customization:** There is no fine-tuning. You adapt Jev to your domain through the `state`, `instructions`, and `criteria` fields.
- **Language:** English works best. Other languages, including CJK scripts, work less well.
- **Data:** Jev is not trained on customer data. Zero data retention is available for enterprise customers.

# TypeSafe API Reference (Summary)

**Not in this page:** the `TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images` header, `assets`, multipart format, the `box` question/answer type, the `jev-preview` / `jev-1.13` / `jev-1.14` aliases, a maximum question count, and any state size limit other than the overall body cap. The page only mentions `jev-latest` and points to a separate Models page for other models and aliases.

## Endpoint and headers
- `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone`
- `Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>`
- `Content-Type: application/json`
- `Content-Encoding` is optional and can be `gzip`, `x-gzip`, or `zstd`.

## Request body
- **`state`** (required): a string, object, or array. This is the content being evaluated, such as text, chat logs, records, or app state.
- **`model`** (required): a string. The docs say to use `"jev-latest"`, which they call the "flagship model". The example responses report `"jev-1.13.0"`.
- **`questions`** (required): a map from IDs you choose to Question objects. Answers come back under the same IDs. The key "is not sent to the underlying model and is not used in inference."

## Request rules
| Rule | Limit |
|---|---|
| Body size | 32 MiB maximum, not counting headers. Exceeding it returns 413. |
| Encoding | UTF-8 JSON with no BOM. |
| Nesting | No more than 64 levels in each of `state`, `instructions`, and `criteria`. |
| Numbers | Must be finite. `NaN`, `Infinity`, and overflow values like `1e400` are rejected. Send large IDs or exact quantities as strings. |

Breaking any rule except body size returns 400.

**Compression:** use a single layer only. The zstd window can be at most 8 MiB. The 32 MiB cap applies both before and after decompression. The SDKs zstd-compress bodies of 1 KiB or more when the runtime supports it. An unsupported encoding or multiple layers returns 415. A malformed compressed body returns 400.

## Question types
Every question has `type` and `instructions`. `instructions` can be a string, object, or array.

Structured instructions let you put the question in one field and supporting data in others. The question then refers to those fields by name in backticks, e.g. "Is the resume for the same person as `potential_duplicate`?"

- **`noul`** (yes/no): `criteria` is optional and takes the form `{ "true": ..., "false": ... }`. Each value can be a string, object, or array.
- **`choice`**: `criteria` is required. It maps each option to a description (string, object, array, or `null`). Up to 255 options are allowed.
- **`score`**: `criteria` is required. It is an ordered array of level descriptions, where position gives the level index starting at 0. Use at least 2 levels; the API accepts up to 10.

Example request (paraphrased):
```json
{
  "state": "Payouts failing for 3 days!",
  "model": "jev-latest",
  "questions": {
    "dept": {
      "type": "choice",
      "instructions": "Which team?",
      "criteria": { "billing": "Payments", "technical": "Bugs" }
    },
    "mood": {
      "type": "score",
      "instructions": "How frustrated?",
      "criteria": ["Calm", "Frustrated", "Very angry"]
    }
  }
}
```

## Response body
- **`model`**: a string.
- **`answers`**: a map keyed by your question IDs.
- **`usage`**: `{ input_tokens, output_tokens }`, both integers.

Each answer type has these fields:
- **noul**: `type` and `noul`, a number from 0 (no) to 1 (yes).
- **choice**: `type`, `choice` (the top option), `probabilities` (option to float, summing to 1), and `confidence` (0–1, derived from the probabilities).
- **score**: `type`, `score`, `legend`, `probabilities`, and `confidence`.
  - `score` is a probability-weighted value, so it can fall between levels (e.g. 1.05).
  - `legend` maps each level string ("0", "1", …) to its description.
  - `probabilities` maps each level string to a float, summing to 1.

## Errors
| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 400 | The request breaks a request rule, or it returns `max_tokens_exceeded` because the input exceeds the model's context length. |
| 401 | The API key is missing or invalid. |
| 413 | The body is over 32 MiB. |
| 415 | The encoding is unsupported, or there are multiple compression layers. |
| 422 | Validation failed, e.g. a missing field or malformed question. The response body names the offending field. |
| 429 | Rate limited. |
| 529 | The service is overloaded. |

For 429 and 529, retry with exponential backoff. The SDKs do this automatically with their default retry policy.

# TypeSafe Score: Guidance Summary

## When to use a Score
Use a Score when the answer sits somewhere on a spectrum that you can describe in steps, such as bug severity or depth of experience. Use a **Choice** for unordered options and a **Noul** for yes/no.

## Request shape
A request has three top-level fields: `state`, `model` and `questions`. Each Score question has:
- `type`: always `"score"`
- `instructions`: what is being rated
- `criteria`: an ordered list of levels, from low to high. You need at least two levels, and the API accepts up to 10.

The question ID is your choice. It isn't sent to the model, and the answer comes back under the same ID.

Illustrative request (my wording, same structure as the docs):
```json
{
  "state": "<content to evaluate>",
  "model": "jev-latest",
  "questions": {
    "bug_severity": {
      "type": "score",
      "instructions": "How severe is the reported issue?",
      "criteria": ["<lowest level>", "<middle level>", "<highest level>"]
    }
  }
}
```

Python SDK equivalent (condensed):
```python
from typesafe_sdk import Score, TypeSafeClient

with TypeSafeClient() as client:
    resp = client.system_one(
        state=ticket_text,
        questions={"bug_severity": Score(instructions="...", criteria=[...])},
    )
    print(resp.answers["bug_severity"].score)
```
Call it through `system_one` or `https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone`.

## Levels
- A level's number is its index in `criteria`, starting at 0.
- The model sees only the descriptions. Each level is "judged on its own against the state."

## Response fields
- **`probabilities`**: one probability per level, keyed by level number as a string. They sum to 1. The Python SDK keys these by integer instead.
- **`score`**: the probability-weighted mean of the level numbers. It ranges from 0 to the top level and can fall between levels. In the docs example, 0×0.0 + 1×0.57 + 2×0.43 = 1.43.
- **`legend`**: maps each level number back to its description, or to the object if you used structured levels.
- **`confidence`**: a value from 0 to 1 based on how the probability is spread. All probability on one level gives 1.0, and wider spread gives lower values. It describes the model's answer, "not a guarantee that the answer is correct."

## Reading a Score
- The same score can come from different distributions. For example, 1.0 can mean everything on level 1, or half on level 0 and half on level 2. Check `probabilities` and `confidence` alongside the score.
- A fractional score is a position, so you can use it directly to rank items by severity. You can also round it to the nearest level when you need one outcome.
- Low confidence usually points to one of three causes:
  - levels that overlap for this input
  - a question that measures several things
  - a state that lacks enough information to place it

## Writing good levels
- **Describe situations, not degrees.** A concrete description gives the model something to match. Something like "Moderately severe" doesn't.
- **Don't rely on numbers.** The model never sees a level's number or its neighbours. Phrases like "worse than previous" and numbers in the text don't help. With criteria `["0","1","2"]`, a cosmetic bug scored 0.55 at confidence 0.33. With descriptive levels, it scored 0.0 at confidence 1.0.
- **Number of levels:** use as many as you can describe distinctly, up to 10. Three is fine.
- **One dimension per question.** Something like "punctual and smart and experienced" mixes three things, which lowers confidence and makes the score less meaningful. Split it into separate Score questions.
- **Give rare extremes their own level.** For example, add "abusive or threatening" above "very angry" so the two don't merge near the top of the scale.
- **No in-between at all?** Use a Choice, or several Noul questions.
- **Test against your own data.** Two wordings of the same scale can behave differently. Higher confidence alone doesn't prove one description is better than another.

## Comparable Scores / composite scoring
1. Split a complex judgment into one Score question per factor and send them all in one request. They are evaluated in parallel, so latency barely changes.
2. Scales of different lengths aren't directly comparable. Normalize each score by dividing by `len(criteria) - 1` so they all run from 0 to 1.
3. Combine the normalized scores with weights that you set in code, and adjust the weights when the rankings don't match your team's judgment.

```python
def normalized(answers, qid):
    top = len(QUESTIONS[qid].criteria) - 1
    return answers[qid].score / top

priority = 0.6*normalized(a, "severity") + 0.3*normalized(a, "frustration") \
         + 0.1*normalized(a, "report_quality")
```
In the docs example, the normalized scores are 0.62, 0.64 and 1.0, which gives a priority of about 0.66. The docs call this the **Composite scoring** pattern.

## Structured levels (objects)
- Start with plain strings.
- If inputs you consider clear keep landing between two neighbouring levels, make each level an object. Use the same field names on every level.

```json
"criteria": [
  {"what": "<level description>", "examples": ["<situation>", "<situation>"]},
  {"what": "...", "examples": ["..."]}
]
```
- `instructions` and each criterion can be a string, an object or an array.
- Examples only help when they resemble your real inputs. On the Safari bug report:

| Level descriptions | Score | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Plain strings | 1.43 | 0.35 |
| A matching example | 1.03 | 0.96 |
| An unrelated example | 1.43 | 0.35 (unchanged) |

- Pick examples whose correct levels you already know, then test the revised descriptions on separate inputs.

## Images in levels
The Score page doesn't mention images. The models summary you provided lists Jev's input as text only.

## Pitfalls (recap)
- Using numeric-only levels
- Combining several dimensions in one question
- Treating the score as a fraction or rate. For example, it doesn't measure the share of customers who lack a workaround.
- Ignoring the distribution behind identical scores
- Combining scales without normalizing them
- Adding filler levels you can't describe distinctly
- Using examples that don't match your real inputs
- Relying on aliases like `jev-latest` when you have tuned confidence thresholds. Pin a versioned model ID instead.

content.thinking:
There's a large uncommitted diff in the repo, so I'll make careful additive edits and avoid committing unless asked. First I should establish a baseline by running the test suite in the background, then look into resvg-js's WebP support and raster embedding.

I'm also noticing the site has persona fitting assets—loop videos, hero webps, backgrounds—for the three included personas. These are tempting to use as persona reference examples, but since they're Baste's own accepted outputs, using them risks biasing new candidates toward convergence rather than preserving diversity, which conflicts with the quality-diversity goal. Persona references should anchor the world and vibe, not dictate the specific visual look, so I need to think carefully about how images get used throughout Jev's decision-making—stylistically, for personas, and as examples.

Right now Jev decisions happen mainly through `evaluateWithTypeSafe`, used for QD evaluation of images and final gating across all asset types, with feature descriptors for QD currently derived from regex over text rather than pixels. I'm checking whether there are other places in the codebase making judgement calls—budget logic, the GUI API, CLI—to make sure I account for all the decision points before redesigning how images feed in.

The key opportunity is giving Jev actual candidate pixels in state—rasters, rendered SVGs, or video frames—so that visualQuality, uniqueness, coherence, usability, and personaAlignment can all be judged directly on the image rather than inferred from text, which the current rubric explicitly avoids by instructing not to claim to see an image at all.

I'm now weighing how to restructure the rubric so it works whether or not pixel evidence is present: since the existing text-only levels (like "no execution detail supports judging composition") don't make sense once real pixels exist, I think the cleanest approach is to keep a backward-compatible text-based rubric export as-is, while adding a parallel pixel-evidence rubric, both still respecting the five-dimension weighting defined in AGENTS.md and the existing test constraints on criteria length and level count.

I'm also thinking through how persona reference images should be structured in state — moodboard pins, brand-kit assets, shipped reference images — each tagged with a note and source, so the personaAlignment prompt can explicitly compare candidate.image against persona.references the way you'd compare a photo to a known reference picture.

For style coherence, I realize suite[].image now gives actual sibling thumbnails, which turns coherence checking into "does this visually belong with the accepted set" rather than a text comparison. I'm also considering treating pinned moodboard references tagged "style" as separate style anchors from persona world references, and noting that stylistic traits like color temperature, density, and abstractness are really QD feature descriptors that could replace the current regex-based approach.

With images, Jev could score color temperature, visual density, and abstractness directly from pixels as parallel cheap questions, each mapping to a fixed number of bins that align perfectly with the archive's dimensions — this fixes the real weakness that QD positions are currently guessed from prompt text alone, making it the most impactful structural fix available.

I'd keep the user override for `options.features` if supplied. For text-only mode, the current regex matching warm/cool color words is crude since prompts already state the axis explicitly — Jev scoring from text directly could be more accurate than this keyword heuristic, though the genome text itself already encodes the feature.

But since existing tests expect exactly 6 questions, changing text-mode behavior risks breaking that assumption, so I'd rather leave text mode unchanged and only expand the richer feature questions in visual mode, since the regex approximation is close enough to the stated intent for text-only cases.

For the examples section, I'm thinking about how upvoted/downvoted assets from feedback memory could become few-shot examples once images are involved, letting a learned-taste score compare candidate images against the user's past preferences directly.

A Choice with options like upvoted-leaning, downvoted-leaning, or neither seems preferable to a binary score, since many candidates won't clearly resemble either group. I'm wary of letting that probability directly bias another score numerically -- the current feedback doc's instruction to nudge personaAlignment by a fixed amount is exactly the kind of LLM-prompt directive a judge wouldn't follow precisely, so it's better to keep raw judgments separate and compose any adjustments explicitly in code.

The AGENTS.md rubric already fixes five weighted dimensions, so adding a sixth would break the documented scheme -- I'm weighing whether taste should instead act as a gate, tie-breaker, or bounded adjustment to personaAlignment similar to the existing text-based guidance.

Thinking through the composite options, I'd compare up to a few upvoted and downvoted example images, then in code nudge personaAlignment up by a small amount for matches and down by a larger amount for mismatches, clamped within bounds -- mirroring the existing learned-preference policy while keeping the five-dimension structure intact and storing the raw judgment for reuse.

I also consider whether other criteria need examples: persona alignment levels don't have real visual analogues for "partial" states, motion style choices could use example filmstrips but synthetic ones likely wouldn't generalize to actual video frames so text descriptions work better, and pet-peeve true/false criteria similarly lack available imagery to draw from.

One idea is using the approved fitting assets per base persona (hero, background, icon, loop) as reference examples of on-persona work, but that risks biasing against the uniqueness criterion which wants distinctness from common templates, not from prior approved work — and those assets live in the site's folder rather than engine data, so I'd hold off on wiring that in.

For video candidates, I'm thinking about extracting frames into state and adding motion-specific visual-mode questions: a motionStyle choice (smooth/snappy/liquid/mechanical/static) compared against the persona's aesthetic profile, a loopSeam check for whether the last frame flows into the first, a motionCalm/backgroundSafe score for how distracting the motion is behind UI content, and a check for text artifacts in frames.

I'm wrestling with where this data flows -- whether to fold it into the five composite dimensions or keep it as raw motion judgments with its own gating policy, like treating visible watermarks or text as a hard gate similar to a pet peeve, while being careful about false positives.

For now, I'll keep gating conservative since this is prototype-stage and overly aggressive gates would drop good assets -- so I'll record new motion checks as tags/improvements rather than gates, and revisit the policy later. Then I want to think through what "better motion primitives" actually means for this design system, given that the current motion tokens are pretty thin -- just a few durations, easings, and a single fade-in keyframe -- so building a richer motion token system seems like the real opportunity.

Mapping out the components: duration tokens (instant through slower, plus an ambient loop period), easing tokens (standard/enter/exit/emphasis/linear, possibly with spring approximations), spring parameters for JS libraries, distance and scale tokens for travel and press/hover effects, stagger intervals for lists, and named choreography recipes like enter, exit, emphasis, hover, press, reveal, and ambient drift.

I'm thinking through persona-specific motion flavors too — a liquid grow/bloom for the cyberbotanist, snappy neon flicker for nightmarketcoder, drifting VHS jitter for liminalweeb, and stepped mechanical motion where appropriate — plus a reduced-motion policy that strips durations and disables ambient effects, and the final export shape as CSS custom properties, keyframes, and utility classes wrapped in a media query.

I also want self-contained specimen examples per persona, possibly extending an existing specimen route in the site, and I should unify the motion language used in `motionPhrase` and `generateVideoPrompt` so mechanical personas stop falling back to a generic "smooth, gradual transitions" description. Finally, I want to tie these motion primitives into Jev's judgments by deriving a persona's motion description (tempo, rhythm, loop period) directly from the primitives for comparison against video frames.

Given how large this scope could get, I should prioritize: Phase A is building a multimodal Jev judge core — preparing and validating images for Jev (PNG/JPEG dimension and pixel limits), handling raster resize/conversion, SVG rasterization via resvg, optional video frame extraction via ffmpeg, and building a multipart request with UUID references while tracking size limits and avoiding duplicates.

Then `evaluateWithTypeSafe` needs to send candidate images and persona/suite references when pixels are available, applying a visual rubric with stylistic and taste scoring, plus motion judgments for video. I also need an `evaluator.images` config option defaulting to "auto" (on for direct TypeSafe, off for hosted gateway) along with a danger-zone header, and an evidence label distinguishing text-only from image-backed evaluations.

For image sourcing, I'm thinking through how persona references flow from moodboard pins or brand kit assets, requiring safe remote fetching via `safeFetchBuffer`. Since `generateAssetSuite` doesn't currently know about moodboards (those live in `.baste/moodboards.json` managed by the GUI/API), I'd add an optional `references` input to `generateAssetSuite`/`EvaluateOptions`, have the GUI pass moodboard references, and consider a repeatable `--reference` CLI flag for parity.

I'm also weighing whether to add an optional `references?: PersonaReference[]` field directly to the Persona type itself, making "persona" images first-class. That type is shared across the projects zod schema, so an optional addition should be backward compatible since the schema strips unknown keys. More fundamentally, I'm trying to pin down what "persona images" should mean to the user — giving an image-capable judge visual grounding in the persona's cultural world, sourced from curated moodboard pins and decomposed brand/site assets.

There's also the versioning registry's cultural image scanner and companion portrait assets to consider, though a character portrait for the persona doesn't capture the aesthetic I'm after — I need to check how `scanCulturalImages` sources its imagery. Beyond that, I'm sketching out the next phase around motion primitives: the motion asset file defining per-style motion primitives and video prompt phrases, plus how motion judgments get evaluated frame-by-frame against that profile.

Given the breadth of this work — tests for multipart requests, image normalization, frame extraction, motion token exports, visual judge fallbacks, plus docs updates — I'm weighing whether this warrants entering plan mode first. The scale and number of design decisions (rubric changes, new gates, type changes, API expansion) lean toward checking in before diving into implementation.

aiTitle: Multimodal image support in jev decisions

content.thinking:
The hosted gateway only works with text fields and sizes its budget off string length, with no support for images—so hosted judging has to stay text-only and I won't route images through it. That's a clear boundary, so now I'm moving into designing the actual approach, grounding decisions in the TypeSafe docs and the existing codebase.

First goal: handling candidate images—PNG/JPEG/WebP outputs, rasterized SVGs via resvg-js, and extracted video frames via ffmpeg—need to attach as images in state.candidate. Second, persona visual references raise harder questions: moodboard pins live in gui/api.ts's in-memory map scoped by account, but the judge in src/evaluation shouldn't import from gui, so I'd need an exposed read function; those references are remote URLs, which means fetching them safely (there's a safeFetchBuffer helper for SSRF protection), though it might be cleaner to have the GUI generate handler resolve references to local buffers before passing them along. There's also a cultural reference image registry to account for.

I'm now weighing persona image sources—local file paths tagged as cultural references, and brand kit assets decomposed via mirrorAssets (og-image, thumbnails)—and thinking the cleanest design is a VisualReference type with id, label/role, path or buffer, and tags, passed through EvaluateOptions.references from the orchestrator. I'm tracing the data flow from generateAssetSuite through evaluateBatch to evaluateWithTypeSafe, and debating whether persona references should just be a new optional field on the Persona type itself, though that's complicated since Persona is shared with site API types and zod schemas, and base personas like cyberbotanist don't currently have any images attached.

I'm also considering adding example images for included personas, but noting that the existing generated outputs under site/public/assets/fittings are outputs, not cultural references, so they wouldn't fit. An alternative is a references option within BasteConfig covering persona, style, and liked/disliked examples, fed by CLI flags or GUI moodboard pins—so I'm sketching out how persona images (cultural refs: film stills, spaces, objects sourced from the culture registry, moodboard, or decomposed brand kits) differ from stylistic images, which represent the visual style of the output itself.

Stylistic images should draw from already-accepted assets for coherence plus moodboard style references, and I'm realizing a token palette swatch (rendered via resvg from the decompose step) could also serve as a stylistic reference for Jev's coherence judgments, though font rendering complicates things so a colors-only swatch makes more sense. Example images would then be few-shot cases drawn from upvoted/downvoted feedback assets or archive elites, possibly used as anchors for score levels — echoing the TypeSafe pattern of comparing a candidate image against a known reference image embedded in the instructions versus the state.

I'm thinking it's cleaner to store references once in persona state and have questions point to them by path rather than resending images per question, and to define Choice or Noul criteria using example pictures (liked/disliked/neither) since that's explicitly supported. I'm also noting that video frame arrays with timestamps could support motion judging, and that box-detection could help locate a focal subject within a safe area.

But the default model is jev-latest (1.13), which doesn't support Box, so sending that question type would likely fail or 400 against the default model. That means the box feature would require a separate request specifically targeting jev-preview, adding complexity and cost considerations.

I'm also thinking about QD features derived from pixels instead of regex over the prompt text — currently textFeatures invents positioning from the prompt, but with actual images, Jev could score color temperature, visual density, and abstractness from real pixel data. That would make the QD archive's map honest, since candidates land in cells based on what they actually look like rather than what was requested, which is a meaningful stylistic improvement worth pursuing.

I'll keep textFeatures always returning the same 3-dimensional contract, falling back from configured options to image evidence to text heuristics as needed, since these are descriptive scores rather than quality signals and shouldn't feed the composite. Next I should think through motion-related judgments for video candidates where frame data is available in state.

For an ambient motion loop, useful questions include detecting a visible loop seam between the last and first frames, and classifying the overall motion character (smooth, snappy, liquid, mechanical, or static) — though I'm unsure how reliably that can be inferred from a handful of still frames versus actual timing and easing.

- cut (snappy): abrupt changes, like reveals; rhythmic (mechanical): repeated regular steps, like machinery. Then the code maps this chosen motion character against the persona's expected motion style—smooth to drift, liquid to flow, snappy to cut, mechanical to rhythmic—turning the probability on that expected option into a "motion fit" signal, a nice example of choice distributions feeding into code policy. There's also a background-safety score asking how much the candidate's movement would distract from interface text placed over it, with levels describing concrete scenarios.

I'm weighing whether this duplicates the existing usability score, which already captures distracting motion, versus having value as a separate reusable motion signal now that frames are part of state. I'm also considering a text/watermark detection check since many video and image prompts specify no legible text or logos, which could be a generic useful gate, though I want to be careful not to add policy gates the user didn't request.

Actually, I'm now worried about the token budget itself — 64k per request but only 32k per question, and if images cost 1-2k tokens each, stacking candidate images, persona refs, examples, and video frames could easily blow past that limit. I need to cap how many images each question pulls in rather than throwing everything at every check.

I'm also estimating image token costs based on a likely similarity to Claude's own vision encoder — if tokens scale roughly with pixel count divided by 750, a downscaled 768px image would cost far less than a full-resolution 1568px one, so shrinking images aggressively seems like the right lever to stay under the per-question cap.

I also need to handle images with extreme aspect ratios: if the shortest side drops below some minimum (~280px) after scaling down the longest side, I should instead scale up so the short side meets that floor, which could mean padding or slight upscaling for very wide or tall images.

For rasterization, I'm considering resvg-js for turning SVG with embedded images into PNGs, but need to confirm it handles WebP data URIs — if not, I'd fall back to ffmpeg or just skip the image. For video evidence, I'd use ffmpeg to extract single frames at specific timestamps via scale and seek flags, needing the video duration first to pick frame times.

I realize ffmpeg absence just means text-only video evidence, clearly labeled. I also note the Docker setup only serves the static site through nginx, not the API. Then I'm checking that feedback memory entries lack a file path for the asset, so to pull images of upvoted/downvoted assets as examples I'd need to resolve the assetId to its actual file by matching it to the filename stem under the output assets directory.

The cleanest fix is to record the resolved asset path directly in the feedback entry at rank time, so the judge can later load it without re-deriving the path — then the judge picks the most recent K upvoted and K downvoted entries with resolvable images, rasterizes them, and feeds them as examples. I'm now sketching a dedicated judge question, `learnedTaste`, asking which set of the user's past ratings the candidate most resembles, with liked/disliked options each carrying their own example images.

Rather than folding this into the existing text-based `learnedPreferences` bias instructions meant for the LLM judge, I think the cleaner approach is to expose taste as its own explicit signal in the result object, keeping the raw judgment separate and reusable rather than baking it into personaAlignment scoring logic.

# Jev 1.13 Known Weak Spots

**Note on images:** The page never mentions images, OCR, fine visual detail, comparing multiple images, spatial reasoning, or frames/sequences. It has no image-specific guidance. The only related item is color, which it discusses as hex/RGB values, not pixels.

## The nine documented failure modes and their mitigations

1. **Literal reading.** The model answers what you wrote, not what you intended.
   - *Mitigation:* "state the exact condition in the `instructions`. Be specific. Put boundary cases in the criteria."
   - For unavoidable interpretation: "split it into two literal questions and combine them in code."

2. **Math and numbers.** "Jev is not a calculator."
   - **Counting** (characters, terms, list items) is unreliable, and errors grow with size. *Mitigation:* "count in code." Ask one question per candidate and sum the results yourself.
   - **Numeric representations and color:** hex and RGB values do worse than English color names, and nearness between values isn't judged reliably. *Mitigation:* "do the conversion in code and pass in either the computed number or a named bucket."
   - **Score math:** don't interpolate exact magnitudes from expectations. Use them only for threshold checks.

3. **Dates and times.** Ordering, distances, and window checks are unreliable, and mixed formats make it worse.
   - *Mitigation:* "Extraction is a judgment, so give it to the model. Arithmetic is not, so keep it in code."

4. **Indirection.** Double negatives and multi-hop reasoning reduce accuracy.
   - *Mitigation:* "write your instructions as directly as possible."

5. **Large or irrelevant state.** Unrelated content distracts the model and causes context rot.
   - *Mitigation:* "retrieve and filter in code first, and send only the fields the question needs." A Noul can also filter for relevance.

6. **Adversarial content.** Injected or misleading text in the state can shift answers.
   - *Mitigation:* "be explicit in the criteria. Test your integration thoroughly before deploying it to many users."

7. **Contradictory instructions and criteria.** An example is mapping `true` to "no."
   - *Mitigation:* "treat the criteria as an extension of the instruction."

8. **Choice option order.** The model tends to favor the first option. The page mentions nothing about the number of options.
   - *Mitigation:* "reorder the options to double check that the answer stays consistent."

9. **Generation.** The model isn't trained to produce text.
   - *Mitigation:* "turn extraction into a [Choice] over the options rather than asking for the value itself."

# Jev-1.13 Weak Spots

1. **Literal reading.** The model takes wording at face value and misses the intent.
   *Mitigation:* Spell out the precise condition and put edge cases in the criteria. If interpretation can't be avoided, "split it into two literal questions and combine them in code."

2. **Math and numbers.** "Jev is not a calculator."
   - **Counting:** Tallies of characters, terms or list items are unreliable, and errors grow with size. *Mitigation:* Count in code, or ask one yes/no question per item and add up the results yourself.
   - **Numeric representations:** Hex or RGB values do worse than English names, and closeness between values isn't judged reliably. *Mitigation:* Convert in code and pass "the computed number or a named bucket."
   - **Score math:** Expectations can't be used to recover exact magnitudes between levels. *Mitigation:* Use scores only for threshold checks.

3. **Dates and times.** Ordering, gaps and window checks are unreliable, especially with mixed formats or relative references. *Mitigation:* Have the model extract date parts as a Choice that includes a "not stated" option, then do all comparisons in code.

4. **Indirection.** Double negatives and multi-hop questions lower accuracy. *Mitigation:* Phrase instructions plainly and refer to the relevant state fields by name.

5. **Large, irrelevant state.** Extra content distracts the model ("context rot") and makes errors harder to trace. *Mitigation:* Filter in code first and send only the necessary fields. A Noul can also screen for relevance.

6. **Adversarial content.** Injected or misleading text in the state can shift answers. *Mitigation:* Make the criteria explicit and test thoroughly before a wide rollout.

7. **Contradictory instructions and criteria.** An example is mapping `true` to "no." *Mitigation:* Treat the criteria "as an extension of the instruction" and keep the wording aligned.

8. **Choice option order.** The model tends to favor the first option. *Mitigation:* Shuffle the options and check that the answer stays the same.

9. **Generation.** The model isn't built to produce text, and chaining Choices to force it is slow and works poorly. *Mitigation:* Get candidates from regex or a generative model, then let Jev pick one through a Choice.

The page's closing reminder also warns against putting several judgments into one question.

## Image Concerns

None of these weak spots concern images. The page never mentions images, OCR, counting objects in pictures, or comparing images.

- **Counting** refers only to text: characters, terms and list items.
- **Colors** come up only as hex or RGB values versus English names, not as pixels or visual content.

I've gathered enough context, so now I'm settling on the design—since the user wants direct implementation, I'll proceed carefully and scope out a module for preparing images, with a function that normalizes a source image into a byte-ready format with configurable options.

I'm thinking through sources: raster files, SVG markup or files, remote URLs, and video frames, each needing their own extraction and sizing pipeline respecting Jev's size limits and fallback behavior when tools like ffmpeg are unavailable. I'm also weighing token economy against resolution choices, since image tokens eat into the context budget and I need a sensible default max side length.

Given typical vision tokenization rates, I estimate I can fit roughly 10-20 images per request within the context window, so I'm setting size caps: candidates at 1024px long side, references at 512-768px, frames at 512px, with count limits across personas, suite images, examples, and video frames. I'm also realizing aspect ratios like banners could shrink below the 280px minimum dimension, so I need logic to either rescale up or letterbox-pad short sides to stay within bounds.

For rendering, I'm planning to embed the raster image inside an SVG and use resvg to decode it into a final PNG output, noting that PNG files for photographic content can get large and JPEG might reduce upload size, though token counts likely scale with pixel dimensions rather than file size.

Since resvg only outputs PNG, and the overall request body is capped at 32MiB, I should budget image sizes carefully—maybe limiting the number and resolution of reference images—rather than switch encoders. For inputs that are already compliant PNG/JPEG within size limits, I could consider passing them through unmodified instead of re-rendering.

Actually, I'll always normalize images to a target size for consistency, though I should note resvg likely doesn't respect EXIF orientation like a browser would, which matters more for web-sourced moodboard photos than generated ones—worth documenting but not blocking. Rendering performance looks solid: resvg takes roughly 400ms to downsample a 2560x1600 PNG to 1024px, which is fine given the QD loop's batch sizes and iteration counts, and reference images can be cached and reused across candidates.

For the cache, I'm thinking of a bounded module-level Map keyed by source plus max dimension, storing a promise for the prepared image so URLs don't get refetched for every candidate.

For the multipart transport, I'm switching from a plain JSON fetch body to multipart/form-data when images are attached to a direct (non-hosted) provider — sending a JSON request part describing the model, state, questions, and asset references, alongside separate binary file parts for each image.

I'm worried that using FormData's auto-generated blob parts will attach a stray filename to the request part, which could make the server's multipart parser misclassify it as a file rather than the JSON payload, so it's safer to construct the multipart body manually the way the SDK does to avoid that filename issue.

But I also realize the test suite mocks fetch by parsing every call's `init.body` as JSON, so sending a Blob body for multipart requests would break those tests since `String(blob)` isn't valid JSON — I need to account for that in how I structure the request.

For tests that don't involve real images, since the mock image generator just writes placeholder bytes rather than a real PNG, image preparation will fail to decode. I need to decide: should that failure be fatal, or should it fall back to text-only evidence for that item? I'm leaning toward falling back silently so existing JSON-based tests still pass, but I'm wary that treating a corrupted candidate image as text-only could be misleading for judging purposes.

I think the honest approach is to fall back to text evidence but explicitly tag it as "text-only" versus "rendered," since Jev images are an experimental, prototype-oriented feature and a prep failure shouldn't block generation outright. I also need to think through whether image evaluation should be opt-in or opt-out by default given its experimental status.

For configuration, I'll default `evaluator.images` to true since the user wants full image evaluation, but add a way to disable it via config or a CLI flag -- something simple like `--no-jev-images` or `--text-judge`, keeping the parsing minimal.

For the hosted gateway path, images aren't supported, so that stays text-only by design -- the judgement ceiling assertion requires a string body, so hosted mode just sends flat JSON text.

Now I'm mapping out where images actually go in the TypeSafe state: the candidate render (normalized raster, composited SVG, or video frame array) gets sent once as shared state, along with persona/style reference images like moodboard pins.

For which references actually get used, I'm leaning toward pinned refs as the primary signal since the Studio copy explicitly promises "pinned references steer generation" -- but I need a fallback for users who never pin anything, so decomposed personas could fall back to brand kit assets like the og image or logo, or cultural image refs pulled from the local versioning registry added via the culture command.

So the priority order for persona images becomes: pinned moodboard refs first, then cultural reference images from the CLI, then brand kit og/logo as a last resort, capped at four with tags attached so the model understands what each image represents. The catch is moodboards live only in the GUI API layer, keyed by account, while the CLI and core module have no awareness of them, so I need a clean way to bridge that gap.

I'm thinking of passing references through `generateAssetSuite` by letting the GUI resolve pinned moodboard refs and the CLI resolve cultural refs plus the local moodboards file, then centralizing the logic in a new module like `src/persona/references.ts` with a `collectPersonaReferences(personaId)` function that reads from the account-scoped moodboards file.

Rather than refactoring `api.ts` into a separate moodboard store module, I'll keep it simpler by handling the lookup directly within the generate handler in `api.ts`.

Now I'm designing the state structure for the multimodal judge, organizing the persona's references, influences, and pet peeves alongside the candidate's image and metadata so the judge can evaluate consistently across questions.

For the actual questions, I'm reworking the existing score dimensions so instructions explicitly reference the rendered pixels when available—personaAlignment now asks how closely the candidate image matches the persona's cultural influences and moodboard references, while visualQuality shifts from text-based criteria to assessing actual execution quality like artifacts, broken composition, or malformed elements in the rendered image.

I'm weighing whether to maintain two parallel question sets—text-only for cases without images versus visual variants—keeping both at five levels so normalization stays comparable, though this means updating test fixtures that currently iterate over the text-only criteria. I'm also considering adding a new image-specific score like matchesReferences, which would judge how closely palette, texture, and composition align with the persona's moodboard, but I need to check how this fits into the existing weighted composite scoring described in AGENTS.md.

Rather than introducing a new composite dimension, reference images should feed into the existing personaAlignment and coherence scores. For learned taste preferences, I'm thinking through whether to add a dedicated score question with example images at each level, since the criteria system supports Choice options, Score levels, and Noul definitions all being illustrated with pictures.

A clean approach would be a `tasteMatch` Noul whose true/false criteria each include example images drawn from the user's liked and disliked assets, asking whether the candidate image resembles the liked set more than the disliked set. The question now is how this signal should feed back into the scoring system — rather than the current text-based LLM bias adjustment to personaAlignment, I want something cleaner for Jev, perhaps a separate `taste` signal.

I'm wary of combining it arbitrarily into personaAlignment with some made-up blending formula, since that bakes policy into code. It might be better framed as a tagging mechanism — e.g., flagging candidates that strongly resemble disliked examples — rather than a hard gate, since I'm trying to figure out what "examples" should actually mean here, given the user wants to leverage images across stylistic, persona, and example-based decisions in jev.

Looking at how TypeSafe uses "examples" in criteria arrays, I'm concluding it means defining options via example images, "stylistic" means judging visual quality/coherence from pixels, and "persona" means representing taste through reference images or moodboards. So the goal is: judge style from pixels, represent persona visually, and feed example images (few-shot) into criteria — and for that third piece, the most meaningful source is the user's own liked/disliked assets, resolving their stored assetId into actual files in the output directory.

I can locate those files by constructing the asset filename pattern from persona id, purpose, and timestamp, then globbing the output folders for matching extensions. Pinned moodboard references give examples of the persona's world, while QD archive exemplars could theoretically serve as per-cell best candidates, though that's less essential — text-based feature levels (color temperature, density, abstractness) are probably sufficient for pixel judgments without needing canonical example images for those specific axes.

Actually, replacing the regex-based text features with real visual measurement from Jev would be a genuine upgrade — the archive cells would reflect what the image actually looks like rather than what the prompt requested, catching cases where the generator ignores the intended style. Jev's probability-weighted Score positions could map onto continuous QD features like color temperature in a measured, not assumed, way.

I also notice prompts.ts already defines TEMPERATURE/DENSITY/RENDERING arrays that step through exactly the levels I'd want as Score criteria, so reusing that vocabulary keeps prompt and scoring language consistent, and I'd map each score range onto the corresponding feature axis — temperature spanning -1 to 1, density and abstractness spanning 0 to 1. The key is writing each level description as a concrete visual situation rather than an abstract degree.

When images exist, features should come from asking Jev's visual Score questions directly against the image; without images, I fall back to textFeatures, and I keep explicit options.features when already supplied so existing tests still behave as before. I'm now considering the token cost implications — since images persist as part of the shared state, I need to understand whether each additional scoring question re-reads the image tokens or reuses the already-encoded state, since that affects how expensive the extra Jev questions become per candidate.

With candidate images, references, examples, and video frames combined, I could easily exceed the 32k per-question budget, so I should keep images small — maybe 512px for references/examples and 768-1024px for the candidate, with video frames even smaller. I'll also cap the total number of images per request and plan a fallback to retry with fewer or smaller images if I hit a max_tokens_exceeded error.

Since this image feature is still experimental and meant for prototypes rather than production, I should make it configurable so it can be opted out of easily.

I should also consider that the hosted gateway likely only accepts text, since its budget check requires a string body, so the hosted path stays text-only while the organic path can carry images. I want the evidence field to track whether judging was "text-only" or used images, and if images were used, record counts per role like candidate, frames, references, suite, and examples.

Now I'm drafting the visual question variants for the five composite dimensions, which trigger when the candidate includes images or frames instead of plain text. For personaAlignment I'm writing a visual version that compares the candidate's pictures against persona references when supplied, and I'm starting to draft the 5-level criteria describing visual quality instead of text quality.

I'm defining visualQuality's five levels, from broken rendering with warped forms up through polished professional execution with crisp detail, then moving on to drafting the uniqueness criterion.

For uniqueness I want to phrase it as how distinct the candidate's visuals are from stock imagery and common template assets, reusing the same text criteria since they work across media. Then I start on coherence, asking how well the candidate's palette, shape, and texture align with the suite and persona aesthetic, falling back to persona aesthetic alone when no suite is supplied.

For usability I need to judge real-world legibility -- icons shown on light/dark backgrounds at multiple sizes, calm space for UI text, and for video, checking that motion doesn't distract. I'm realizing the instructions should probably be tailored per asset type since the question set is built per request, so for SVGs specifically I'd want the candidate image shown at several pixel sizes on different backgrounds.

For the pet peeve question, I want to judge whether the candidate's visuals (not just its prompt) exhibit any listed pet peeve, treating the image state as evidence rather than instruction. I'm also sketching new visual-only questions that would only trigger when pixels are present, like scoring stylistic axes such as color temperature, visual density, and abstractness derived from the prompt definitions.

I'm also considering a hygiene check for unwanted text—watermarks, logos, garbled letters—since prompts explicitly forbid UI text, but I'm wary of over-gating: a night-market scene with legible neon signage in Chinese characters is legitimate content, not a failure mode, so a strict reject rule would wrongly penalize it.

Gate-rejected assets get dropped from the suite entirely, and for QD they map to -Infinity quality so they never enter the archive. I'll add an explicit `overlaidText` gate for image/video (skipping SVG, since glyphs may be legitimate there), but keep the threshold stricter than 0.5—maybe 0.7—to avoid false positives wrongly tanking a whole run.

Actually, rather than a separate Noul gate for text, it might be simpler to just let garbled-text concerns surface through the existing visualQuality/usability criteria rubric, since garbled text is already called out there. That avoids introducing a second, differently-calibrated threshold that would look arbitrary next to the 0.5 convention.

But a dedicated signal is cheap and reusable, so I'll keep it — reported as a tag, but only used as a hard gate for the explicit brief exclusions (no overlaid text, watermarks, captions, logos) mentioned in the image/video prompts, gating at the same 0.5 threshold as the other pet peeve checks for consistency.

I'll call it `overlay` (question id `hasOverlay`), asking whether the candidate has lettering, a watermark, or a border/frame over the picture, excluding in-scene signage. For video, "no text, no characters" extends similarly. For SVG I'll skip this check, since our own board compositing with light/dark grounds could get misdetected as an unwanted border or frame.

Padding is another concern — our still-fitting logic adds letterbox padding with neutral ground only when a side falls below 280px after scaling, which could also look like an unwanted border, but this is rare enough in normal aspect ratio ranges that I'll not worry about it further.

Now I'm turning to the motion primitives for video frames — defining a `motionStyle` choice across the four motion languages, each pulling frame descriptions from a motion language map, plus a "still" option.

I'm weighing how reliable this motion judgment really is: with only five stills sampled roughly 1.25s apart, distinguishing "snappy" from "smooth" is weak at best — it's a perceptual best-effort cue rather than a hard gate, so I'm leaning toward treating it as reported signal data rather than feeding it directly into persona alignment scoring.

I'm also considering loop seam detection, comparing first and last frames to judge whether an ambient loop would appear seamless, and motion amount, which ranks visual change across frames from "practically still" through "subtle drift," "moderate motion," "strong motion," to "chaotic."

For UI backgrounds, subtle-to-moderate motion is ideal, though usability scoring already captures distracting motion, so this signal is mostly informative rather than a separate score. I'm thinking about how to surface these motion signals — loop seam, motion amount, motion style — without expanding the five-dimension composite, perhaps by reporting them separately and using thresholds to generate specific improvement suggestions like flagging a mismatched loop seam.

Actually, we do have the site's three loop videos, but they're AI-generated attempts at the persona's style, not verified exemplars — I don't know if they truly match the labeled motion style, so using them as scoring criteria examples is risky since examples only work when their correct level is already known. So that approach is out.

What I really need is a motion specimen page per persona demonstrating enter/exit/hover/press/emphasis/ambient/stagger with that persona's tokens — that's the real "examples for motion" designers and developers would want, and it maps naturally onto a Motion panel in the Studio tokens tab. I could also expose this via CLI as a `--format motion` export that writes a self-contained HTML specimen demonstrating each primitive with the persona's palette and fonts.

But the cleanest path is probably having the Studio tokens tab render live, interactive examples directly from the tokens JSON using the Web Animations API, since the motion primitives are already stored in WAAPI-compatible keyframe format — the Studio can just call `element.animate()` with each primitive's keyframes, duration, easing, and iteration settings to produce real, working demos using the same data developers consume.

This would require updating the shared API types for motion tokens, regenerating demo data, and reworking the tokens tab UI, with verification across desktop and mobile viewports — worthwhile but substantial, so I'll finish the backend judge work first before touching the site. I also want to reconsider how learned-preferences text is passed into state, including any embedded scoring-bias instructions, and now I'm turning to how rated example assets should be resolved from a persona's feedback entries.

I need to grab up to three liked and three disliked recent examples with resolvable images, then decide where they live — either as criteria on a dedicated taste judgment or as a `learnedExamples` field in state that personalAlignment can reference. Following the pattern of defining choice options by example pictures, I think the cleanest design is a Choice judgment asking which set of rated examples the candidate resembles more, with liked/disliked/neither options each carrying example images, so the resulting probabilities give a direct P(liked) vs P(disliked) signal.

I'm now thinking about how to apply that signal: rather than leaving it as loose LLM guidance, I could encode the existing policy numerically in code — adjusting personaAlignment by +0.1 times P(liked) minus 0.15 times P(disliked), clamped to [0,1] — which mirrors the documented bias policy but executes it deterministically. The raw score should still be preserved separately from the adjusted criterion value, and I need to consider whether porting the OpenAI judge's text-based policy into code like this is overengineering or actually the right level of explicitness.

For the Choice format itself, I realize it only makes sense when there are at least two options, so I need to handle cases where only liked or only disliked examples exist by pairing with a "neither" option. Then for persona references, I'm mapping out the sources — moodboard images stored in the GUI's account-scoped JSON store, pinned then sorted by recency — and realizing the evaluation module shouldn't import directly from the GUI API, so I'll need a small accessor module to read the moodboard file independently.

Since the moodboard key logic (combining account key and board id) is duplicated if I just read the file separately, I'm considering extracting moodboard persistence into its own shared module that both the GUI API and the judge can use, which means refactoring the existing moodboard code out of gui/api.ts into something like a `loadMoodboard` function that reads fresh from the file each time.

Beyond moodboards, I'm also thinking about brand kit local assets—og images, thumbnails, logos—as good persona references when decomposing personas, and I need to use them when they're present.

I should avoid creating the DB as a side effect — only read it if `.baste/versions.db` already exists. For remote moodboard URLs, I'd need to fetch over the network safely using something like `safeFetchBuffer` with SSRF protection, a size cap, and a timeout, caching results per process.

That stills.ts change on disk is just from my earlier python edit, so that's expected. Now I need to design the reference loader module and think through the structure of the multimodal judge request, including how persona state gets shared across questions to keep things efficient.

I'm now estimating total token cost across candidate, reference, suite, and frame images against the 64k/32k context limits to figure out how many images is actually safe to include per request.

Since state is shared across questions but each question still needs to fit under 32k tokens, I need to keep image sizes modest — candidate at 1024px long side, references and suite images at 512px, and examples/frames around 384-512px while respecting the minimum 280px short-side constraint for different aspect ratios.

For robustness, I'm also planning a fallback for when the request exceeds token/size limits: if a 400 or 413 error occurs mentioning tokens or size, retry once with only the candidate image, dropping references, suite images, and examples.

I don't want image failures to kill an entire run given the experimental nature of this feature, so for other 4xx errors (excluding auth/rate-limit ones), I'll fall back to text-only evaluation but tag the evidence as "images-rejected" so the degradation is visible rather than silent — careful not to let this become a way of inventing passing scores for what's really a service failure.

I realize the rubric wording needs to differ depending on whether pixels are available — the current instructions explicitly forbid claiming to see an image, but when an image is present the judge should actually evaluate the rendered result. So I need two variants of each question, visual and text-only, keeping the same 0–4 scale so the composite score stays normalized and comparable within a run.

Instead of regex-derived textFeatures, I'm defining pixel-based questions mapping directly to the archive's descriptors: color temperature, visual density, and abstractness, each scored and converted into the corresponding feature value for its bin count. This is a real upgrade since it positions the archive by what the image actually looks like rather than by what the prompt merely requested.

I want caller-supplied features to still take priority when given explicitly. For the level descriptions, I need concrete, vivid anchors (cold palette vs. hot palette, etc.) across five levels so scoring is unambiguous. I'm also wondering whether to anchor each level with example images, though it's unclear where such reference images would come from—maybe the user's own rated set could serve that purpose.

I'm now thinking about a reference-match criterion that compares the candidate image's visual language against a set of reference images, with levels ranging from "contradicts the references" to "could pass as the same body of work." This only applies when references exist, so I need to decide whether it folds into persona alignment or stands as its own weighted criterion in the composite score.

Since the state already includes references, the persona alignment question automatically sees them too, so a separate match score risks duplicating that signal rather than adding something new — though there may still be value in exposing the raw affinity score separately for transparency, without adding a whole new dimension to the evaluation interface.

I'm deciding to keep the fixed 5-dimension EvaluationCriteria rather than add a 6th, since it's used across GUI, feedback, and QD and adding one would be invasive. Instead I'll make personaAlignment and coherence's instructions reference images directly—persona images and the suite's rendered look—and treat the user's thumbs up/down history as a labeled example set that could inform a Choice-style question.
